cells.tense: You're moving toward a light you picked, and the weighing sits level in your hands.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you're aiming at, then ask what would make it fair between you. Weigh what they say and let it change the split.
cells.core:
You're moving toward something you picked, and you know how to weigh things fairly. Fairness here isn't a rule you follow. It's something you keep doing — noticing what's out of proportion, adjusting it, letting the adjustment stand even when it costs you. That's the work, and you're in it.

The direction you're facing and your sense of what people are owed run the same way for you, which is rarer than it sounds. What it costs to keep: calibrating runs on attention, and attention runs down, so there's a plain limit to how much you can spend without getting thin. Let part of the weight land on someone else instead of balancing it all yourself. One way: say what you're aiming at and let them have a say in what's fair.
cells.sheetLine: The weighing stays level because you keep at it.
cells.verb: Picking the light to move toward and going that way
cells.place: Where things get weighed and set level between people

cells.tense: You'll have the fairness settled before anyone in the room has asked.
cells.ask: Pick one disagreement about what's fair and leave it alone for a day. Ask what they noticed and write down the first thing that lands.
cells.core:
You're bracing toward a fairness that hasn't happened yet. The splitting gets done ahead of time, scores settled before anything's gone wrong, and the weighing gets checked so often nobody can move near it.

What you're aiming at is real: things should come out fair. That direction is yours. The bracing is what costs you — defending a call you haven't made. Choosing which way to go and running ahead to make sure nobody can shift the frame are two different moves.

When you stop settling things ahead of the moment, your read on what's off still lands on its own. Before you adjust what's out of proportion, let one thing stay crooked for a day. You'll still see it. You'll just see it from here.

cells.tense: You stood at that door and did not say which way you were going.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person which way you were heading before things went quiet, and that you're still heading there.
cells.core:
There's a direction you were moving toward, and after something behind you made it hard to say out loud, you stopped saying it. The aim didn't leave. You just stopped standing behind it. When a room works out what's fair now, you're not really in the weighing.

That's not a missing sense of what's right. It's a scale you set down, and the eye for it went quiet with it. So it looks like not knowing what you're for. It's closer to not having said it in a while.

Things you used to tend can go well with less strain than you remember. Let some of your energy go there instead of straight back at the scale. Tell one person which way you were heading, and notice that the direction was yours the whole time.
cells.sheetLine: You put the scale down and the weighing stopped.

cells.tense: You're setting things level between people and calling it the situation.
cells.ask: Name one adjustment you made for someone as your call, out loud. If it was doing their work, stop making it.
cells.core:
The scale gets leveled between people around you and you'd say it leveled on its own. Your hand is on it — in what you let pass, what you rebalance without announcing, which way the room ends up facing. It works. You don't say so.

What runs underneath is steady and shared: strength that holds people up without pressing them down, and your part in it goes unnamed. You just call it nothing, or the way things are. That leaves the same work running where nobody asked whether it should.

The simpler move: part of what you rebalance is your call, not a requirement. Name one of those adjustments as yours. If the other person is carrying their own weight fine, put it down.

attempts.check: The record does not support saying the person compares their life to anyone else's, so that claim is out. A reader could reasonably say they weigh things carefully on purpose and enjoy it, which every core lets them say — a core that only accuses is a core that fails. The ask lands after the read and stays useful if the read is wrong: each puts something concrete in front of one person and lets it be answered. The sentence that serves me most is any line about 'the scale' — the noun for the seat's mechanism that the person never used — so it stays in my own description of what the act is, not in their mouth.
